newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Bass Strait pipeline offer made - AGL.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Bass Strait pipeline offer made - AGL.

text.p: The backers of the proposed "logical link" gas pipeline between Victoria and New South Wales have made a "very competitive" offer to Bass Strait producers to pipe gas to NSW, the Australian Gas Light Co said on Thursday.

The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd, in partnership with Vancouver-based Westcoast Energy, currently plans to build its own 740km east coast pipeline, taking Bass Strait gas from the Victorian plant at Longford to Sydney and Port Kembla.
The BHP pipeline is one of two rival gas links planned between the two states in line with the opening up of competition in the gas industry.

The other is the 146 km Wodonga-Wagga Wagga "logical link" pipeline, which is to be built by East Australia Pipeline Ltd (EAPL), owned 51 percent by AGL and 49 percent by foreign investors, and GTC, which is owned by the state of Victoria.

AGL chairman Len Bleasal said he understood EAPL and the Victorian government have made a joint offer to BHP and Bass Strait partner Exxon Corp for transportation from the Bass Strait terminal at Longford to various points in NSW.
"It's very competitive with any other proposals, and the Victorian government strongly supports the offers that have been put forward," Bleasel told Reuters.
"Our view is that the Victorian government is very keen to see it brought up through the GTC/EAPL system," he said.
"That means they believe they have got a price before Esso/BHP that says it's cheaper to come that way than build their own pipeline."
The GTC/EAPL link, which would cost about A$125 million in its first stage, was planned to be completed by April 1998.
Bleasel said it could carry about 20 petajoules of gas per annum in its first stage, and could be increased to carry between 70 and 90 petajoules.
BHP currently uses less than 10 petajoules a year at its Port Kembla plant but this could rise to around 20 petajoules with the construction of a cogeneration plant.
EAPL general manager Jim McDonald told Reuters the interconnect between the Victorian and the NSW gas systems would offer the best outcome for energy reform in Australia's south-east.
"We have made an offer to Esso/BHP in conjunction with the Victorian government and we believe it is competitive with any options available to them," he said.
